'''''Amaranthus palmeri''''' is a species of edible [[flowering plant]] in the [[amaranth]] genus. It has several common names, including '''carelessweed''',<ref name="USDA">{{PLANTS|id=AMPA|taxon=Amaranthus palmeri|access-date=7 January 2016}}</ref> '''dioecious amaranth''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''Palmer's amaranth''', '''Palmer amaranth''', and '''Palmer's pigweed'''.

It is native to most of the southern half of North America. Populations in the eastern United States are probably [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]]. It has also been introduced to Europe, Australia, and other areas. The plant is fast-growing and highly competitive.

==Uses==
[[File:Amaranth muesli.jpg|thumbnail|Amaranth muesli mix]]
The leaves, stems, and seeds of Palmer amaranth, like those of other [[amaranth]]s, are edible and highly nutritious.<ref name="USDA" /><ref name="NAED">{{cite web|url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Amaranthus+palmeri|title=Native American Ethnobotany Database}}</ref> Palmer amaranth was once widely cultivated and eaten by Native Americans across North America, both for its abundant seeds and as a cooked or dried green vegetable.<ref name="NAED" /> Other related ''Amaranthus'' species have been grown as crops for their greens and seeds for thousands of years in Mexico, South America, the Caribbean, Africa, India, and China.

The plant can be toxic to non-ruminant livestock animals due to the presence of [[nitrate]]s in the leaves.<ref name="Cornell">{{cite web|url=https://www.ansci.cornell.edu/plants/php/plants.php?action=indiv&byname=scientific&keynum=12|publisher=Cornell University Department of Animal Science|title=Plants Poisonous to Animals}}</ref> Palmer amaranth has a tendency to absorb excess soil [[nitrogen]], and if grown in overly fertilized soils, it can contain excessive levels of nitrates, even for humans. Like spinach and many other leafy greens, amaranth leaves also contain [[oxalic acid]], which can be harmful to individuals with kidney problems if consumed in excess.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.upmc.com/patients-visitors/education/nutrition/Pages/low-oxalate-diet.aspx|publisher= University of Pittsburgh Medical Center|title=Low Oxalate Diet|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Citation needed|date=July 2026|reason=source used is unverifiable, as dead}}

Because of its toxicity to [[livestock]], and scarce familiarity in the United States with the uses of amaranths as food, Palmer amaranth is rarely consumed as of 2020,{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}{{Update inline|date=July 2026|?=y}} despite its ubiquity and [[Drought tolerance|resistance to drought]]. Unlike the grain and leaf amaranths of other regions, it has not been cultivated or further improved by recent [[Plant breeding|agricultural breeding]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/nexus/Amaranthus_spp_nex.html|publisher=Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products|title=Amaranthus species}}</ref>{{Additional citation needed|date=July 2026|reason=the source here does not necessarily prove that there are no cultivars, nor does it demonstrate notability/due weight}} As a result, the primary economic importance of Palmer amaranth to American farmers has been as a [[noxious weed]] and a competitor to more marketable crops, rather than as a crop in its own right.<ref name="USDA" /> 

==As a weed==
Palmer amaranth is considered a threat most specifically to the production of [[cotton]] and [[soybean]] crops in the southern United States. In 2001, Palmer amaranth was found in the southern quarter of Illinois and appeared to be moving to northern Illinois in 2006.<ref>{{cite web|author1=Hager, Aaron|author2=Sprague, Christy|url=http://bulletin.ipm.illinois.edu/pastpest/articles/200105l.html|title=Waterhemp--Biology, Identification, and Management Considerations|publisher=University of Illinois Extension|date=27 April 2001|access-date=7 May 2017|archive-date=15 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210515210535/http://bulletin.ipm.illinois.edu/pastpest/articles/200105l.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Herbicide resistance===
In many places, the plant has developed [[Pesticide resistance|resistance]] since at least 2006 to [[glyphosate]], a widely used broad-spectrum [[herbicide]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.salon.com/2008/08/27/monsantos_bane/|author=Andrew Leonard|title=Monsanto's bane: The evil pigweed|work=Salon.com|date=27 August 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.france24.com/en/20090419-%E2%80%98superweed%E2%80%99-explosion-threatens-monsanto-heartlands-|author=Clea Caulcutt|title='Superweed' explosion threatens Monsanto heartlands|publisher=France 24|date=19 April 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Culpepper AS, Grey TL, Vencill WK, Kichler JM, Webster TM, Brown SM|display-authors=etal|title=Glyphosate-resistant Palmer amaranth (Amaranthus palmeri) confirmed in Georgia|journal=Weed Sci|volume=54|issue=4|pages=620–626|year=2006|doi=10.1614/WS-06-001R.1|s2cid=56236569}}</ref> Glyphosate-resistant pigweed not only dominates in cotton fields, but also has wide-ranging effects on other crops and productions.<ref name="herbicide">{{cite web|author=Roy Roberson|title=Herbicide resistance may change future of row crop farming in Southeast|publisher=Southeast Farm Press|date=8 August 2006|url=http://www.southeastfarmpress.com/herbicide-resistance-may-change-future-row-crop-farming-southeast}}</ref>

In 2014, the [[Texas Department of Agriculture]] asked the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] for permission to use the restricted chemical propazine on 3 million acres (1.2 million hectares) of cotton threatened by Palmer amaranth.<ref>{{Cite news|url = http://southwestfarmpress.com/cotton/tda-seeking-emergency-approval-propazine|title = TDA seeking emergency approval for propazine|last = Hawkes|first = Logan|date = 23 June 2014|work = South West Farm Press|access-date = 29 July 2014}}</ref> The request was denied due to unacceptable risks to drinking water.<ref>{{Cite news|url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/epa-denies-texas-emergency-weedkiller-request-1406053913|title = EPA Denies Texas Emergency Weedkiller Request|last = Bunge|first = Jacob|date = 22 July 2014|work = Wall Street Journal|access-date = 29 July 2014}}</ref>

In 2019, [[Kansas State University]] researchers documented a population of Palmer amaranth with resistance to [[2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid|2,4-D]] and [[dicamba]] in Kansas. Previously, Palmer amaranth in Kansas has developed resistance to ALS, atrazine, glyphosate, and HPPD herbicides—mesotrione, Huskie, Laudis, Impact, and Armezon—leaving growers with very few [[postemergence]] options to manage this weed.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Peterson |first1=Dallas |last2=Jugulam |first2=Mithila |last3=Shyam |first3=Chandrima |last4=Borgato |first4=Ednaldo |title=Palmer amaranth resistance to 2,4-D and dicamba confirmed in Kansas |url=https://webapp.agron.ksu.edu/agr_social/eu_article.throck?article_id=2110 |access-date=4 March 2019 |work=K-State Extension Agronomy eUpdate |agency=Kansas State University Research and Extension |issue=734 |date=1 March 2019}}</ref>

An [[Arkansas]] population has developed [[fomesafen]] resistance.<ref name="Salas-et-al-2016">{{cite journal|last1=Salas|first1=Reiofeli A|last2=Burgos|first2=Nilda R|last3=Tranel|first3=Patrick J|last4=Singh|first4=Shilpa|last5=Glasgow|first5=Les|last6=Scott|first6=Robert C|last7=Nichols|first7=Robert L|title=Resistance to PPO‐inhibiting herbicide in Palmer amaranth from Arkansas|journal=[[Pest Management Science]]|volume=72|issue=5|year=2016|pages=864–869|issn=1526-498X|doi=10.1002/ps.4241|pmc=5069602|pmid=26817647|publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]]}}</ref>

[[Gene drive]] technologies could provide a countermeasure: A gene drive agent could engineer ''A. palmeri'' to become glyphosate-sensitive again. Such a wide-ranging application of the technology should{{Editorialising|date=July 2026}} be carefully considered, though.<ref name="Chen-Wang-et-al-2019">{{cite journal | last1=Chen | first1=Kunling | last2=Wang | first2=Yanpeng | last3=Zhang | first3=Rui | last4=Zhang | first4=Huawei | last5=Gao | first5=Caixia | title=CRISPR/Cas Genome Editing and Precision Plant Breeding in Agriculture | journal=[[Annual Review of Plant Biology]] | publisher=[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]] | volume=70 | issue=1 | date=2019-04-29 | issn=1543-5008 | doi=10.1146/annurev-arplant-050718-100049 | pages=667–697 | pmid=30835493| s2cid=73471425 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Growth===
Palmer amaranth may be the most aggressive pigweed species with respect to growth rate and competitive ability.<ref name="reduce">{{cite web|author = Paul Hollis|url=http://www.southeastfarmpress.com/management/resistant-pigweed-reduce-seed-bank|title=Resistant pigweed: "Reduce seed bank"|publisher=Southeast Farm Press|date=18 September 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref> Palmer amaranth in particular is highly competitive. It will outgrow cotton and is much more efficient. Growers of crops have not been able to provide adequate moisture to offset prolonged temperatures above {{ convert | 85 | F | C }} with a {{ convert | 112 | F | C }} [[heat index]]. In these conditions, many herbicides break down over time and Palmer amaranth will keep growing. It can grow from {{convert | 2 | to | 5 | in | mm }} in three days, or less.<ref name="herbicide" /> In only a few weeks, it can grow from {{ convert | 12 | to | 18 | in | mm }} compared to cotton at {{ convert | 5 | to | 8 | in | mm }}.<ref>{{cite web|author=James Langcuster|title=Resistant pigweed: the ultimate monkey wrench|publisher=Southeast Farm Press|url=http://www.southeastfarmpress.com/management/resistant-pigweed-ultimate-monkey-wrench|date=14 October 2009}}</ref>

===Spread===
Pollen is most commonly spread by wind.<ref name="herbicide" /> The male produces the pollen and the female plant produces the seed. The wind carries the pollen from resistant male plants to female plants. In addition, the seed is spread by traditional means, such as harvesting, inadequate cleaning of equipment, and the spreading of contaminated materials, such as manure.<ref name="reduce" />

In 2014, North Dakota State University's "ND Weed Control Guide" selected ''Amaranthus palmeri'' as "weed-of-the-year" to raise awareness about its "potentially devastating impact."<ref name="agcanada_2015">{{cite web|url=http://www.agcanada.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/GNN150120.pdf |title=Palmer amaranth is a looming concern: This aggressive, herbicide resistance weed has been travelling north, and may be in our fields soon |author=Julienne Isaacs |date=January 20, 2015 |access-date=7 August 2015 |publisher=Grain News |volume=41 |number=2}}</ref>{{rp|5}} In 2015, Palmer amaranth was chosen as "weed-of-the-year" for the second year in a row as a "proactive approach to prevent Palmer amaranth establishment in North Dakota."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ag.ndsu.edu/weeds/weed-of-the-year-files/palmer-amaranth-2|title=Palmer Amaranth – Weed of TWO Years – 2014-2015|date=26 October 2016|publisher=North Dakota State University|access-date=26 October 2016}}</ref> As alien, this species was first found in South Africa in March 2018, with further records in different regions of the country as well as in northern Botswana in March 2020. It is considered a naturalized weed which invades both [[ruderal species|ruderal]] and segetal (growing in cornfields) plant communities.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.reabic.net/journals/bir/2021/1/BIR_2021_Sukhorukov.pdf|title=First records of ''Amaranthus palmeri'', a new emerging weed in southern Africa with further notes on other poorly known alien amaranths in the continent.|date=2021|publisher=BioInvasions Records 10(1): 1-9}}</ref>
